final_proof:
For a subset A of S_1, write f[A] for its direct image. Because the restriction of the direct-image map is a surjection from tau_1 onto tau_2, it is in particular a well-defined map into tau_2 and is onto. Consequently,

    tau_2 = {f[U] : U in tau_1}.                                  (1)

We first prove that tau_2 is a topology on S_2. Since tau_1 is a topology, the empty set and S_1 belong to tau_1. Moreover, f[emptyset] = emptyset, and surjectivity of f gives f[S_1] = S_2. Thus (1) implies that emptyset and S_2 belong to tau_2.

We will use the following consequence of bijectivity. If V is in tau_2, then (1) gives some U in tau_1 such that V=f[U]. Since f is injective,

    f^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[f[U]] = U;                                (2)

indeed, membership from right to left is immediate, while if x is in f^{-1}[f[U]], then f(x)=f(u) for some u in U, and injectivity gives x=u in U. Hence f^{-1}[V] belongs to tau_1 for every V in tau_2.

Now let C be any family of members of tau_2, and put

    W = union_{V in C} f^{-1}[V].

Every set occurring in this union lies in tau_1 by (2), so W belongs to tau_1 because tau_1 is closed under arbitrary unions. Direct image commutes with arbitrary unions, and, because f is surjective, f[f^{-1}[V]]=V for every V subseteq S_2. Therefore

    f[W] = union_{V in C} f[f^{-1}[V]] = union_{V in C} V.

By (1), f[W] belongs to tau_2. Thus tau_2 is closed under arbitrary unions.

Finally, let V_1,V_2 be in tau_2. By (2), the sets f^{-1}[V_1] and f^{-1}[V_2] lie in tau_1, so their intersection lies in tau_1. Since preimages commute with intersections and f is surjective,

    f[f^{-1}[V_1] intersect f^{-1}[V_2]]
      = f[f^{-1}[V_1 intersect V_2]]
      = V_1 intersect V_2.

Equation (1) therefore shows that V_1 intersect V_2 belongs to tau_2. Hence tau_2 is also closed under finite intersections (the nullary case is S_2, already handled). This proves that (S_2,tau_2) is a topological space.

It remains to prove homeomorphism. The map f is bijective by hypothesis. It is continuous because, for every V in tau_2, equation (2) says that the preimage f^{-1}[V] lies in tau_1. Let g:S_2 to S_1 be the inverse bijection f^{-1}. For every U in tau_1, the preimage of U under g is

    g^{-1}[U] = f[U],

and this belongs to tau_2 by (1). Thus g is continuous as well. Therefore f is a continuous bijection with continuous inverse, so f is a homeomorphism from (S_1,tau_1) to (S_2,tau_2). Consequently, (S_2,tau_2) is a topological space homeomorphic to T_1.
